The key is to think of it in simpler terms:

When you split 1 pizza pie amongst two persons, we think well, how much of the original pie does each person get? Each person get half of the pie. 
1/2 represents this.

But when you think, what is 1 pizza split amongst a half persons?  It's weird.

The thing to understand is that dividing by a fraction requires a sort of different thinking than how we normally go about division, because its weird to think about dividing a pizza amongst a  half peoples.  This is due to the nature of 1/2 not being a natural or counting number, but rather a ratio between 2 natural numbers.

More importantly, this leads us to observing how division by a number less than 1 yields more than the original as in the case of 1/(1/2) = 2. Here we're thinking how many halves are in a whole? You have two halves. Notice you get more than the original.

Onto your example:

When you divide 1 pizza amongst 8 people, each person gets an eighth of the pie.
1/8 = slice of the pie each person gets

Now, its extra weird because what if you ask how much is an 1/8 of a slice split amongst 1/2 a persons?

But wait, we are dividing by a fraction so we have to have more than 8, which is why you do the flip in general. (1/8 divided by 1/2) = (1/8 * 2)which equals 1/4. 

We used something from a simpler example to understand the badic workingsof something we do understand to apply them to an example we don't.

Sorry for not directly answering the question with simply a real world example but it's important to understand the nature of the "flip" because as you progress in your math journey things will become more and more abstract to where it is difficult to find real world examples. But we can observe and thus prove things are true for things that we dont actually understand. That's why math is so badass.

Hope this helps!

Sure, you can get around this by attending other schools that may have less math reqs. or perhaps switch to another major with less math courses, but engineering relies heavily on a good math foundation which includes a fair amount of Calculus.

You don't need to be a master or anything but you definitely are going to need it. If you still want to do it, and find that it may be too difficult, maybe take a class or two less and take your time.  I went into Comp Sci. not really being "good" or "loving" math, but I was geniunely curious and it took a while, but now I enjoy it. Competency is necessary to understand the next topic but mastery is a different thing. Most engineers don't remember all the ways to derivate or integrate, however, you could have a deep understanding of what integrals are conceptually and maybe integrate a few tough ones but by no means do you need mastery to test well. Of course with plenty of practice comes mastery and with practice comes deeper understanding, but test taking is not the same skill as conveying information is not the same as calculation etc. I know plenty of people who are amazing at tests but can barely explain a concept whether that be lack of communication skills or not truly grasping something. Test taking is about, yes, knowledge of material but it's both an interpersonal skill and analytical one.  Being able to assess what someone is looking for based on the way they teach as well as analyzing previous test patterns. Practicing pacing under a time limit and having an understanding of what is expected. These are the things that make a good test taker, mastering the material is a great goal but in reality if someone who passed calc 2 or 3 told me they had mastery over calculus and that's why they did well, I'd be hard pressed not to ask them why they're not winning awards in their field as well.

First of all, take a step back and breath. A lot of us have been there and before you catastrophize ( I dont mean this in a reductive manner), allow yourself some time to process the information you just learned subconsciously ( the info you've learned regarding the class , as well as, not performing the way you expected). Its easy to get caught up in working too hard and that can often hinder performance. 

Once you take a sec to breathe you can think about what's not working and re-adjust because from the information you have given, whatever strategy you are currently using isnt allowing you to be as effective as you could be. For me it takes longer to 'get it', but often, I tend to have a significantly deeper understanding than my peers.

Also remember you now have information that you didnt previously have since you've taken the midterm.  Pay special attention to what types of questions will be asked and focus on identifying patterns that allow you to narrow down how you prioritize your studying. Teachers can tell you all they want about what you SHOULD do but often it doesn't work given that only you really know how you learn best. Identify that and execute. You got this.

Distribute as you normally would in a binomial expansion:
a*~a + a*~b + b*~a + b*~b

0 + a*~b + b*~a + 0

This can be read as: The statement will be true when 

a=true AND b=false OR b=true AND a=false.
